title: Blood molecules found in a 115-million-year-old dinosaur bone — a first, with a debate
excerpt: Scientists report the first direct molecular evidence of blood-derived compounds inside structures that look like red blood cells in a 115-million-year-old dinosaur fossil from Brazil. One independent expert is not convinced.
content:
A 115-million-year-old fossil dinosaur bone from Brazil contains tiny structures resembling red blood cells — and molecular traces of blood, an international research team reports in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

The study, published November 2, 2026, is the first direct molecular evidence of compounds from dinosaur blood preserved within structures that look like red blood cells, according to the team led by Kliti Grice, an organic and isotope geochemist at Curtin University in Perth, Australia.

The specimen is a partial hind limb of Aratasaurus museunacionali, a small meat-eating theropod from the Romualdo Formation in northeast Brazil. Inside the bone's vascular canals — the tiny channels that once held blood vessels — the team found numerous mineralized structures about 23 micrometers long and 20 micrometers wide, and chemical analysis detected heme molecules, a component of hemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying protein in blood. The researchers detected heme B and a chemically altered relative called 3,8-diethyl heme B.

How the team tested whether it is really blood

The central question was whether the structures were true biological remains or something that formed later as the bone turned to stone. The team says the structures appear only inside the vascular canals, where red blood cells sit in living animals — the surrounding sediment contained none of them. The chemistry also differed sharply: the sediment mostly held compounds from plants and bacteria, while the bone showed a distinct signature dominated by heme molecules.

The researchers propose that the dinosaur was buried quickly in an environment with little oxygen and abundant microbial activity, which slowed decay. A manganese mineral called hausmannite may also have helped, acting somewhat like an antioxidant and stabilizing the sensitive molecules. The team stresses the blood did not stay fresh: the cells turned into minerals during fossilization.

"We have not found a vial of dinosaur blood," the researchers note. "What we are seeing is a mineral and molecular echo of ancient biology." No intact ancient collagen protein or dinosaur DNA was recovered.

The debate

Not everyone is convinced. Mary Schweitzer, a molecular paleontologist at North Carolina State University who was not involved in the study, disputes the identification of the microscopic structures, citing their shape, size and lack of a nuclear bulge. The fossil cell-like structures also look somewhat larger and more rounded than red blood cells in modern birds and crocodilians — the dinosaurs' closest living relatives.

That disagreement is how science is supposed to work: one team publishes its evidence, and other experts test it. If the interpretation holds, it suggests fragile biological material can survive far longer than many scientists assumed — the previous record for blood molecules was roughly half as old. If it does not, the chemistry still tells researchers something new about how fossils preserve, and mislead.
